Likewise, the measures proposed and carried out for protection and management of those species and subspecies will undoubtedly include some that have not yet been 'proposed, and the resulting economic environment may be broadened. This broadening will not be a monotonic function of the numberes of listed species and subspecies, however. We can anticipate that as the list increases, particularly in the Group 2 category, the overlap in ranges of listed species will increase and sites supporting more than one species will emerge. probability is that isolate species from diverse taxonomic groups will share the same range. Thus, an area which contains an isolated population of one taxa is more likely to support isolates of other taxa than is the surrounding habitat due to its historical and ecological characteristics. As this situation developes, species-specific recovery programs will be supplanted to some degree by habitat management programs with a consequent reduction in cost per species and an increased benefit per program. Area-wide habitat management programs, furthermore, are more likely to produce benefits in non-endangered species aspects and further economic benefits can be realized through enhanced aesthetic, recreational, and sport values. The potential of the proposed legislation for maximizing multi-species program development with corresponding decreases in the cost/benefit ratio is an important aspect of its economic impact.
